# Cūḷasāropama Sutta (MN 30 (PTS MN i 198))

**ID:** MN 30 (PTS MN i 198)
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Cūḷasāropama Sutta
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** The Shorter Simile of the Heartwood
**PTS:** MN i 198
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/mn30

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Cūḷasāropama Sutta* ("The Shorter Discourse on the Simile of the Heartwood") is the thirtieth discourse of the *Majjhimanikāya* [Buswell & Lopez 2014; Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995]. Set at Jeta's Grove in Sāvatthi, the sutta recounts an exchange between the Buddha and the brahmin Piṅgalakoccha, who inquires whether the leaders of rival ascetic orders are all fully awakened as they claim [Buswell & Lopez 2014; Hazra 1994; Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995]. In response, the Buddha employs the extended simile of a great tree possessed of heartwood (*sāra*), sapwood, inner bark, outer bark, and twigs and leaves to illustrate the spiritual path and correct practice (*brahmacariya*) [Anālayo; McTighe; Rogell 2003].

Sharing its core analogy and conclusion with the preceding *Mahāsāropama Sutta* (MN 29), the discourse warns disciples against mistaking intermediate achievements for the true goal of the holy life [Anālayo; Pande 1974; Rogell 2003]. Gain, honour, and renown are compared to twigs and leaves; moral virtue to the outer bark; concentration to the inner bark; and knowledge and vision (*ñāṇadassana*) to the sapwood [Hazra 1994; Rogell 2003; Saitanaporn 2009]. Whereas MN 29 depicts monks becoming intoxicated with these stages, MN 30 emphasizes complacency through slackening and failing to make further effort [Durham 2004; Rogell 2003]. The sutta outlines states higher and more sublime than knowledge and vision—specifically the eight meditative absorptions (*jhāna* and immaterial attainments) and the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*)—before concluding that only unshakeable deliverance of mind (*akuppā cetovimutti*) constitutes the heartwood and final culmination of the teaching [Griffiths 1986; Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995; Rogell 2003].

A full parallel to the discourse exists in Chinese translation in the *Ekottarāgama* (EĀ 43.4) [Buswell & Lopez 2014; SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus records substantial Pali-internal text reuse with MN 29 (645 matches, over 115,000 shared characters, prominently §7.1–8.7 ↔ MN 29 §2.9–2.19), as well as significant shared phrasing with passages in the *Aṅguttaranikāya* (AN 4, AN 9, AN 10, AN 3, AN 5), MN 79, DN 6, and SN 35 [DharmaNexus]. Cross-language alignments computed by DharmaNexus match formulaic meditative sequences with Sanskrit and Tibetan treatises, notably the *Śrāvakabhūmi*, the *Arthaviniścayasūtra-nibandhana*, and the *Daśottarasūtra* [DharmaNexus]. Modern English translations have been published by I. B. Horner, Bhikkhu Ñāṇamoli, and Bhikkhu Sujato [SuttaCentral].

**Sources**

- [SuttaCentral] SuttaCentral record for MN 30 — Basic bibliographic data, English title, blurb, list of translations, and parallel in EĀ 43.4.
- [DharmaNexus] DharmaNexus matches for MN 30 — Pali-internal text reuse with MN 29 and other Nikāya texts, and cross-language alignments with Sanskrit and Tibetan works.
- [Anālayo] Bhikkhu Anālayo, From Craving to Liberation: Excursions into the Thought-world of the Pali Discourses (1) — Explains the simile of the tree and mistaking subsidiary factors for the final goal of heartwood.
- [Buswell & Lopez 2014] Robert E. Buswell Jr. and Donald S. Lopez Jr., Princeton Dictionary of Buddhism (2014) — Contextual details on the setting, the interlocutor Piṅgalakoccha, the question about rival teachers, and the Chinese Ekottarāgama parallel.
- [Durham 2004] Jeffrey Sean Durham, Certainty’s Seal: Dynamics of Religious Assurance in Indian Buddhism (2004) — Notes the sutta's depiction of resting on laurels and slackening due to fame.
- [Griffiths 1986] Paul J. Griffiths, On Being Mindless: Buddhist Meditation and the Mind-Body Problem (1986) — Discusses higher states beyond knowledge and vision, including the formless attainments and cessation.
- [Hazra 1994] Kanai Lal Hazra, Pāli Language and Literature (1994) — Summary of the conversation with Piṅgala Koccha and immutable deliverance as the true reward.
- [McTighe] McTighe, Mentoring in the Majjhima Nikaya — Discusses the discourse's teaching to Piṅgalakoccha on Brahmafaring using the simile of the pith.
- [Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995] Bhikkhu Ñāṇamoli and Bhikkhu Bodhi, The Middle Length Discourses of the Buddha (1995) — English title, setting at Jeta's Grove, opening with Piṅgalakoccha, and identification of unshakeable deliverance of mind as the goal.
- [Pande 1974] Govind Chandra Pande, Studies in the Origins of Buddhism (1974) — Compares MN 29 and MN 30 as two closely related versions of the same discourse.
- [Pye] Michael Pye, Skilful Means: A Concept in Mahayana Buddhism — Discusses the simile of the pith and spiritual disciples failing to grasp what matters.
- [Rogell 2003] Sharda Rogell, Pressing Out Pure Honey: A Practitioner’s Study Guide (Majjhima Nikāya) (2003) — Compares MN 29 and MN 30, detailing the tree simile elements, phrasing differences, and the absorptions as higher states.
- [Saitanaporn 2009] Phramonchai Saitanaporn, Buddhist Deliverance: A Re-evaluation of the Relationship Between Samatha and Vipassanā (2009) — Cites the sutta on ñāṇadassana as a meditative experience and the lack of conceit regarding attainments.
